medical.title: Mobile CT lung cancer screening expands access for underserved populations in Brazil
medical.summary: Mobile low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening can reach high-risk and socially vulnerable populations in resource-limited settings, according to initial results from the Third Brazilian Early Lung Cancer Trial (BRELT3) presented at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC).

medical.title: New method explores how mitochondrial tRNA changes can reshape immune cell behavior
medical.summary: For generations, scientists have looked to the genetics inside immune cells for ways to improve how the body fights disease.

medical.title: Abdominal aortic aneurysms can cause years of anxiety, even without symptoms
medical.summary: Some people describe it as a ticking time bomb. Others learn to live with information they can neither see nor feel but cannot forget. This is what it can mean to be diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm: a swelling in the body's main artery that becomes more likely to rupture as it grows, despite causing no symptoms.

medical.title: New ablation approach improves outcomes for persistent atrial fibrillation
medical.summary: Atrial fibrillation is the most common cardiac arrhythmia and increases the risk of conditions such as stroke and heart failure. An established treatment is catheter ablation, in which physicians use thin catheters to create small scars in heart tissue to block the electrical signals that cause the arrhythmia. Despite treatment, many patients with the more difficult-to-treat form, persistent atrial fibrillation, experience recurrence.

medical.title: Volatile work hours cut access to employer health insurance, study finds
medical.summary: In the 46 years since Dolly Parton wrote the workers' anthem "9 to 5," American jobs, and access to employment-based health insurance, have changed a lot.

medical.title: Volunteers intentionally exposed to influenza to advance vaccine research
medical.summary: For the first time in Canada, researchers are intentionally exposing healthy volunteers to influenza under carefully controlled conditions to establish a research model that could accelerate the evaluation of future influenza vaccines and strengthen pandemic preparedness.

medical.title: Leukemia study highlights need to standardize testing
medical.summary: Multiparametric flow cytometry—a test that is widely accessible, cost-effective and timely—can find one cancerous cell hidden among thousands of healthy cells following treatment for acute myeloid leukemia.

medical.title: Poor sleep in one partner can affect both partners' diets, new study finds
medical.summary: Poor sleep is known to lead to poor diet quality. But as a new Concordia-led study of cohabiting couples shows, poor sleep can affect not only an individual's food choices but also their partner's choices. Because couples who sleep together often eat together, one partner's unhealthy food choices can have a ripple effect on the other's eating habits, the researchers say.

medical.title: Drug improves sexual function for patients with depression, study finds
medical.summary: Patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and an inadequate response to standard antidepressants who received add-on treatment with the drug lumateperone had significantly improved sexual function, according to a new study led by a University of Virginia School of Medicine researcher.

medical.title: Reducing infections after heart surgery could save Medicare $441 million per year
medical.summary: Where a patient undergoes heart surgery can significantly affect their risk of infection following the procedure, with some patients facing more than double the risk of others, according to a new Michigan Medicine study.

medical.title: A blind retina isn't silent—and its noise may hinder efforts to restore sight
medical.summary: When retinitis pigmentosa takes a person's sight, the standard clinical test goes flat: no response, no signal, nothing. Yet the retina behind that flat line is anything but quiet.

medical.title: New culture membrane mimics the native intestinal environment
medical.summary: The human intestine is a soft, flexible tissue. Yet the environments traditionally used to culture intestinal cells in the laboratory are strikingly different from those found in the body. Conventional culture platforms are made of synthetic materials that are far stiffer than native intestinal tissue. Could we instead provide cells with an environment that more closely resembles the intestine?

medical.title: Emergency C-section infections decline as azithromycin use rises following previous clinical trial results
medical.summary: Infection can develop in up to 10–20% of patients after a cesarean delivery, and the risk nearly doubles for those who have an unplanned cesarean delivery, such as those performed during labor.

medical.title: Watching sports on YouTube doesn't mean you'll get off the couch, new research shows
medical.summary: YouTube has become a go-to platform for sports content, offering far more than traditional game broadcasts and sports news. Alongside highlights and commentary, viewers can find content tailored to their interests, including home-training tips, diet and nutrition advice, and information about sports equipment.

medical.title: New study sheds light on dementia among Indigenous Bolivians
medical.summary: In two Indigenous communities living preindustrial lifestyles in the Bolivian Amazon, dementia is remarkably uncommon. However, a new longitudinal study reveals why earlier estimates told only part of the story.

medical.title: Having a bad hair day? My new research might help
medical.summary: Think about the last time you looked in the mirror and sighed at the sight of your hair. Maybe it was frizzing, flattening, graying, thinning or simply refusing to do what you wanted. For many people, hair comes with a running commentary—a private, near-constant negotiation that we rarely stop to notice, let alone question.

science.title: Adaptive crystal can selectively capture CO₂ and recognize similar molecules
science.summary: Chemical separation can be energy-intensive when molecules have similar sizes and properties. Researchers from Shibaura Institute of Technology, Japan, have now developed an interlayer adaptive crystal that changes its spacing to recognize specific molecules.

science.title: Magnets could help quantum computers talk to each other, says researcher
science.summary: Xufeng Zhang is using magnets to make computers more power efficient at the quantum level. The Northeastern professor of electrical and computer engineering recently published two papers highlighting small-scale magnetic systems he and his team developed that could help make computers much more power efficient in the future.

science.title: Home advantage or pastures new? High-Arctic shorebirds rarely return to the same breeding area
science.summary: Shorebirds are capable of some of the longest migrations on Earth, yet most return year after year to the same area to breed. Coming back has distinct advantages, including knowing the best spots to feed or roost, having information about where predators lurk, and—hopefully—finding last year's partner again.

science.title: Great Salt Lake's ancient past reveals how quickly fresh water can disappear
science.summary: From a mountainside overlooking Utah's Great Salt Lake, a time traveler turning back the clock 20,000 years would watch a dramatic transformation of the landscape. The shallow, salty lake below would swell into an immense body of fresh water, at one point reaching nearly 1,000 feet (305 meters) deep and covering more than 10 times the lake's modern area. Mountain ranges would become islands, and the new shoreline would move far beyond its current boundary.

science.title: Not all roads lead to Rome: Research challenges what we think we know about Roman roads
science.summary: A multidisciplinary team of researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark, Queen Mary University of London and other European institutions analyzed a data set representing almost 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles) of Roman roads across the former empire, creating the most detailed quantitative picture yet of how the Roman road network was structured.

science.title: Mitotic chromosomes may assemble from pre-existing chromatin 'building blocks' during cell division
science.summary: Inside each human cell, about 2 meters (6.6 feet) of genomic DNA must be accurately copied and equally transmitted to two daughter cells during cell division. To achieve this, the copied DNA is condensed into thick, short structures called mitotic chromosomes. However, how chromatin is organized and condensed to form mitotic chromosomes has long remained a major question in genetics and cell biology.

science.title: Is science journalism dying? Comparing a 'science crash' 40 years ago to today
science.summary: When two popular science magazines—out of about 17 in circulation—ceased publication in the same year, one commentator said, "The science magazines didn't shake out. They fell apart." The general manager of one of the failed magazines said, "There was a perception that they were irrelevant." One of the publishers remembered being in a "state of shock" as the failures emerged.

science.title: Record-breaking levels of plastic found in seabirds, with almost 900 pieces found in one bird alone
science.summary: For more than a decade, it was thought that the world's most plastic-polluted birds couldn't get any more contaminated by the man-made material. But then, from 2023–2026, the record was broken every single year.

science.title: 3D food printing of balanced vegetarian dishes from rice and lentil flours
science.summary: Rice and lentils are a pairing that goes a long way back, whether as khichdi in India or mujaddara in the Middle East. On its own, each is a source of incomplete protein, short on certain essential amino acids—but paired together, they fill each other's gaps, and lentils also blunt white rice's high glycemic index.

science.title: Greenhouse gas benefits of agricultural irrigation far outweigh emissions costs, study finds
science.summary: Irrigating U.S. crops prevents higher greenhouse gas emissions by avoiding land conversion, new research by Colorado State University shows. Agricultural irrigation allows the United States to grow more food on less land. If irrigation were suddenly shut off, the land-use change required to make up for lost yields would produce significantly more greenhouse gas emissions than irrigation emits—363 times more.

science.title: Heat-stable enzyme from deep-sea microbe turns nitrogen gas into ammonia
science.summary: Microorganisms can do remarkable things—for example, nitrogen fixation, the conversion of nitrogen gas (N₂) into a form that organisms can use. Although nitrogen gas makes up around 78% of Earth's atmosphere, plants and animals cannot directly use it.

science.title: How advertising turns our insecurities into profit—and how you can resist the manipulation
science.summary: Have you ever bought something not because you wanted it, but because you were afraid of what might happen if you didn't? Maybe you worried about looking older, falling behind at work or simply not fitting in.

science.title: Avoiding a sticky situation: How cells stop messenger RNAs from clumping together
science.summary: Messenger RNA, or mRNA, is best known for carrying genetic instructions from DNA to the cellular machinery that makes proteins. But all RNA molecules have another, less appreciated property: They are naturally sticky.

science.title: Frontline safety concerns mount among property managers, new survey shows
science.summary: Safety and security challenges are creating unprecedented strain for frontline property management professionals, according to a new bilingual survey conducted by Portland State University's Center for Real Estate. Initiated after industry partners raised alarms about changing workplace conditions, the study offers insight into the daily risks experienced by property management staff at multifamily and commercial properties.

environment.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
environment.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

environment.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
environment.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

environment.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
environment.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

environment.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
environment.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

environment.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
environment.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

environment.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
environment.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

environment.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
environment.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

environment.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
environment.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.

mix_items.title: Mobile CT lung cancer screening expands access for underserved populations in Brazil
mix_items.summary: Mobile low-dose computed tomography (LDCT) screening can reach high-risk and socially vulnerable populations in resource-limited settings, according to initial results from the Third Brazilian Early Lung Cancer Trial (BRELT3) presented at the International Association for the Study of Lung Cancer (IASLC) 2026 World Conference on Lung Cancer (WCLC).

mix_items.title: New method explores how mitochondrial tRNA changes can reshape immune cell behavior
mix_items.summary: For generations, scientists have looked to the genetics inside immune cells for ways to improve how the body fights disease.

mix_items.title: Adaptive crystal can selectively capture CO₂ and recognize similar molecules
mix_items.summary: Chemical separation can be energy-intensive when molecules have similar sizes and properties. Researchers from Shibaura Institute of Technology, Japan, have now developed an interlayer adaptive crystal that changes its spacing to recognize specific molecules.

mix_items.title: Abdominal aortic aneurysms can cause years of anxiety, even without symptoms
mix_items.summary: Some people describe it as a ticking time bomb. Others learn to live with information they can neither see nor feel but cannot forget. This is what it can mean to be diagnosed with an abdominal aortic aneurysm: a swelling in the body's main artery that becomes more likely to rupture as it grows, despite causing no symptoms.

mix_items.title: Magnets could help quantum computers talk to each other, says researcher
mix_items.summary: Xufeng Zhang is using magnets to make computers more power efficient at the quantum level. The Northeastern professor of electrical and computer engineering recently published two papers highlighting small-scale magnetic systems he and his team developed that could help make computers much more power efficient in the future.

mix_items.title: New ablation approach improves outcomes for persistent atrial fibrillation
mix_items.summary: Atrial fibrillation is the most common cardiac arrhythmia and increases the risk of conditions such as stroke and heart failure. An established treatment is catheter ablation, in which physicians use thin catheters to create small scars in heart tissue to block the electrical signals that cause the arrhythmia. Despite treatment, many patients with the more difficult-to-treat form, persistent atrial fibrillation, experience recurrence.

mix_items.title: Volatile work hours cut access to employer health insurance, study finds
mix_items.summary: In the 46 years since Dolly Parton wrote the workers' anthem "9 to 5," American jobs, and access to employment-based health insurance, have changed a lot.

mix_items.title: Home advantage or pastures new? High-Arctic shorebirds rarely return to the same breeding area
mix_items.summary: Shorebirds are capable of some of the longest migrations on Earth, yet most return year after year to the same area to breed. Coming back has distinct advantages, including knowing the best spots to feed or roost, having information about where predators lurk, and—hopefully—finding last year's partner again.

mix_items.title: Volunteers intentionally exposed to influenza to advance vaccine research
mix_items.summary: For the first time in Canada, researchers are intentionally exposing healthy volunteers to influenza under carefully controlled conditions to establish a research model that could accelerate the evaluation of future influenza vaccines and strengthen pandemic preparedness.

mix_items.title: Great Salt Lake's ancient past reveals how quickly fresh water can disappear
mix_items.summary: From a mountainside overlooking Utah's Great Salt Lake, a time traveler turning back the clock 20,000 years would watch a dramatic transformation of the landscape. The shallow, salty lake below would swell into an immense body of fresh water, at one point reaching nearly 1,000 feet (305 meters) deep and covering more than 10 times the lake's modern area. Mountain ranges would become islands, and the new shoreline would move far beyond its current boundary.

mix_items.title: Leukemia study highlights need to standardize testing
mix_items.summary: Multiparametric flow cytometry—a test that is widely accessible, cost-effective and timely—can find one cancerous cell hidden among thousands of healthy cells following treatment for acute myeloid leukemia.

mix_items.title: Poor sleep in one partner can affect both partners' diets, new study finds
mix_items.summary: Poor sleep is known to lead to poor diet quality. But as a new Concordia-led study of cohabiting couples shows, poor sleep can affect not only an individual's food choices but also their partner's choices. Because couples who sleep together often eat together, one partner's unhealthy food choices can have a ripple effect on the other's eating habits, the researchers say.

mix_items.title: Drug improves sexual function for patients with depression, study finds
mix_items.summary: Patients with major depressive disorder (MDD) and an inadequate response to standard antidepressants who received add-on treatment with the drug lumateperone had significantly improved sexual function, according to a new study led by a University of Virginia School of Medicine researcher.

mix_items.title: Reducing infections after heart surgery could save Medicare $441 million per year
mix_items.summary: Where a patient undergoes heart surgery can significantly affect their risk of infection following the procedure, with some patients facing more than double the risk of others, according to a new Michigan Medicine study.

mix_items.title: Not all roads lead to Rome: Research challenges what we think we know about Roman roads
mix_items.summary: A multidisciplinary team of researchers from Aarhus University in Denmark, Queen Mary University of London and other European institutions analyzed a data set representing almost 300,000 kilometers (186,000 miles) of Roman roads across the former empire, creating the most detailed quantitative picture yet of how the Roman road network was structured.

mix_items.title: A blind retina isn't silent—and its noise may hinder efforts to restore sight
mix_items.summary: When retinitis pigmentosa takes a person's sight, the standard clinical test goes flat: no response, no signal, nothing. Yet the retina behind that flat line is anything but quiet.

mix_items.title: Mitotic chromosomes may assemble from pre-existing chromatin 'building blocks' during cell division
mix_items.summary: Inside each human cell, about 2 meters (6.6 feet) of genomic DNA must be accurately copied and equally transmitted to two daughter cells during cell division. To achieve this, the copied DNA is condensed into thick, short structures called mitotic chromosomes. However, how chromatin is organized and condensed to form mitotic chromosomes has long remained a major question in genetics and cell biology.

mix_items.title: New culture membrane mimics the native intestinal environment
mix_items.summary: The human intestine is a soft, flexible tissue. Yet the environments traditionally used to culture intestinal cells in the laboratory are strikingly different from those found in the body. Conventional culture platforms are made of synthetic materials that are far stiffer than native intestinal tissue. Could we instead provide cells with an environment that more closely resembles the intestine?

mix_items.title: Is science journalism dying? Comparing a 'science crash' 40 years ago to today
mix_items.summary: When two popular science magazines—out of about 17 in circulation—ceased publication in the same year, one commentator said, "The science magazines didn't shake out. They fell apart." The general manager of one of the failed magazines said, "There was a perception that they were irrelevant." One of the publishers remembered being in a "state of shock" as the failures emerged.

mix_items.title: Record-breaking levels of plastic found in seabirds, with almost 900 pieces found in one bird alone
mix_items.summary: For more than a decade, it was thought that the world's most plastic-polluted birds couldn't get any more contaminated by the man-made material. But then, from 2023–2026, the record was broken every single year.

mix_items.title: 3D food printing of balanced vegetarian dishes from rice and lentil flours
mix_items.summary: Rice and lentils are a pairing that goes a long way back, whether as khichdi in India or mujaddara in the Middle East. On its own, each is a source of incomplete protein, short on certain essential amino acids—but paired together, they fill each other's gaps, and lentils also blunt white rice's high glycemic index.

mix_items.title: Emergency C-section infections decline as azithromycin use rises following previous clinical trial results
mix_items.summary: Infection can develop in up to 10–20% of patients after a cesarean delivery, and the risk nearly doubles for those who have an unplanned cesarean delivery, such as those performed during labor.

mix_items.title: Greenhouse gas benefits of agricultural irrigation far outweigh emissions costs, study finds
mix_items.summary: Irrigating U.S. crops prevents higher greenhouse gas emissions by avoiding land conversion, new research by Colorado State University shows. Agricultural irrigation allows the United States to grow more food on less land. If irrigation were suddenly shut off, the land-use change required to make up for lost yields would produce significantly more greenhouse gas emissions than irrigation emits—363 times more.

mix_items.title: Watching sports on YouTube doesn't mean you'll get off the couch, new research shows
mix_items.summary: YouTube has become a go-to platform for sports content, offering far more than traditional game broadcasts and sports news. Alongside highlights and commentary, viewers can find content tailored to their interests, including home-training tips, diet and nutrition advice, and information about sports equipment.

mix_items.title: Heat-stable enzyme from deep-sea microbe turns nitrogen gas into ammonia
mix_items.summary: Microorganisms can do remarkable things—for example, nitrogen fixation, the conversion of nitrogen gas (N₂) into a form that organisms can use. Although nitrogen gas makes up around 78% of Earth's atmosphere, plants and animals cannot directly use it.

mix_items.title: How advertising turns our insecurities into profit—and how you can resist the manipulation
mix_items.summary: Have you ever bought something not because you wanted it, but because you were afraid of what might happen if you didn't? Maybe you worried about looking older, falling behind at work or simply not fitting in.

mix_items.title: New study sheds light on dementia among Indigenous Bolivians
mix_items.summary: In two Indigenous communities living preindustrial lifestyles in the Bolivian Amazon, dementia is remarkably uncommon. However, a new longitudinal study reveals why earlier estimates told only part of the story.

mix_items.title: Avoiding a sticky situation: How cells stop messenger RNAs from clumping together
mix_items.summary: Messenger RNA, or mRNA, is best known for carrying genetic instructions from DNA to the cellular machinery that makes proteins. But all RNA molecules have another, less appreciated property: They are naturally sticky.

mix_items.title: Frontline safety concerns mount among property managers, new survey shows
mix_items.summary: Safety and security challenges are creating unprecedented strain for frontline property management professionals, according to a new bilingual survey conducted by Portland State University's Center for Real Estate. Initiated after industry partners raised alarms about changing workplace conditions, the study offers insight into the daily risks experienced by property management staff at multifamily and commercial properties.

mix_items.title: Having a bad hair day? My new research might help
mix_items.summary: Think about the last time you looked in the mirror and sighed at the sight of your hair. Maybe it was frizzing, flattening, graying, thinning or simply refusing to do what you wanted. For many people, hair comes with a running commentary—a private, near-constant negotiation that we rarely stop to notice, let alone question.

mix_items.title: Indigenous land back in Chile brings mixed bag of environmental outcomes: Study
mix_items.summary: Indigenous land restitution in Chile came with a mixed bag of environmental outcomes and did not boost natural forest cover, according to a new study published in Nature Sustainability. While the return of ancestral lands gave the Indigenous Mapuche communities in southern Chile greater control over how their land was used — leading to an […]

mix_items.title: 1.4-million-year-old footprints reveal a surprisingly large human relative
mix_items.summary: Ancient footprints in Kenya reveal that eight Paranthropus boisei may have traveled together 1.4 million years ago, with some individuals reaching surprisingly large, human-like body sizes. The tracks offer a rare glimpse of their social behavior and suggest these extinct human relatives may have lived in more complex groups than previously thought.

mix_items.title: Seven new frog species were hiding beneath Madagascar’s forest floor
mix_items.summary: Scientists have discovered seven new species of Madagascar’s elusive diamond frogs, using DNA from modern and century-old museum specimens to solve a long-running biological puzzle. The findings reveal surprising hidden diversity and could help protect these little-known amphibians as their forest habitats disappear.

mix_items.title: Ancient Egyptian princesses were buried with weapons. Their bones reveal why
mix_items.summary: Weapons buried with ancient Egyptian princesses may have been more than ceremonial decorations. Researchers studying royal mummies from Dahshur found bone changes consistent with years of archery and other strenuous weapon use. Several women also showed evidence of healed injuries, suggesting surprisingly active lifestyles that may have included hunting or military training.

mix_items.title: A Manhattan-sized ice island just broke free from Greenland
mix_items.summary: A huge section of Greenland’s Petermann Glacier has snapped off, forming an ice island about the size of Manhattan. Satellites watched cracks spread rapidly before the 76-square-kilometer slab finally broke free on August 4. It is the glacier’s biggest calving event since 2012, and scientists say two even larger pieces could eventually follow. The rare Arctic iceberg will now be tracked as it drifts, breaks apart, and potentially affects shipping routes.

mix_items.title: Atomic catalyst unlocks the hidden value of plant waste
mix_items.summary: Scientists have created a highly efficient catalyst that breaks down stubborn lignin from plant waste into useful chemicals under relatively mild conditions. By revealing exactly how the catalyst works at the atomic level, the discovery could help turn forestry and agricultural waste into renewable building blocks for fuels, plastics, and other materials.

mix_items.title: Scientists find hidden “highways” guiding animal evolution
mix_items.summary: A sweeping analysis of thousands of animal genomes suggests that chromosomes do not evolve randomly but instead follow a limited number of irreversible “evolutionary highways.” These one-way genetic changes preserve clues to more than 600 million years of animal history and could even help researchers explore where evolution may head next.

mix_items.title: NASA finds Earth microbes could survive on the Moon
mix_items.summary: NASA scientists found that microbes brought by astronauts could survive in cold, shadowed niches around the Moon’s South Pole, potentially complicating future searches for pristine lunar chemistry. Some refuges may be no larger than a footprint, while one hardy fungus could even withstand limited exposure to sunlight.
